[tools]
# Please also keep the version aligned in the go.mod file
go = { version = '1.26.0', postinstall = "go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@latest && go install gotest.tools/gotestsum@latest" }
golangci-lint = '2.10.1'
shellcheck = 'latest'
tmux = 'latest'

[tasks.fmt]
description = "Run gofmt"
run = "gofmt -s -w ."

[tasks.test]
description = "Run tests"
run = "go test ./..."

[tasks."test:integration"]
description = "Run integration tests"
run = "go test -tags=integration ./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/..."

[tasks."test:ci"]
description = "Run all tests (unit + integration) with race detection"
run = "go test -tags=integration -race ./..."

[tasks.build]
description = "Build the CLI"
run = """
VERSION=$(git describe --tags --always --dirty 2>/dev/null || echo "dev")
COMMIT=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo "unknown")
go build -ldflags "-X github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/versioninfo.Version=${VERSION} -X github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/versioninfo.Commit=${COMMIT}" -o entire ./cmd/entire
"""

[tasks."build:all"]
description = "Build for all platforms using goreleaser"
run = "goreleaser build --snapshot --clean"

[tasks."completions"]
description = "generate entire shell completions"
quiet = true
run = """
rm -rf completions
mkdir completions
for sh in bash zsh fish; do
    go run ./cmd/entire/main.go completion "$sh" >"completions/entire.$sh"
done
"""

[tasks.dup]
description = "Check for code duplication (threshold 50, with summary)"
run = """
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Create temp files with proper extensions (works on both Linux and macOS)
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
config="$tmpdir/config.yaml"
json_out="$tmpdir/output.json"

cat > "$config" << 'YAML'
version: "2"
linters:
  default: none
  enable: [dupl]
  settings:
    dupl:
      threshold: 50
YAML

# Run with JSON output for summary, text output for details
golangci-lint run -c "$config" --new=false --max-issues-per-linter=0 --max-same-issues=0 \
  --output.json.path="$json_out" --output.text.path=/dev/stderr ./... 2>&1 || true

# Print summary grouped by file
echo ""
echo "=== Duplication Summary (by file) ==="
if command -v jq &>/dev/null && [ -s "$json_out" ]; then
  jq -r '.Issues // [] | group_by(.Pos.Filename) | map({file: (.[0].Pos.Filename | split("/") | .[-1]), count: length}) | sort_by(-.count) | .[] | "  " + (.count|tostring) + " " + .file' "$json_out" 2>/dev/null || echo "  (no issues)"
else
  echo "  (install jq for summary)"
fi

rm -rf "$tmpdir"
"""

[tasks."dup:staged"]
description = "Check duplication in staged files only (threshold 75, same as CI)"
run = """
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Get staged Go files, preserving paths with spaces using null delimiters throughout
if ! git diff --cached --name-only -z --diff-filter=ACM | grep -z '\\.go$' | grep -zq .; then
  echo "No staged Go files to check"
  exit 0
fi
echo "Checking staged files for duplication..."
git diff --cached --name-only -z --diff-filter=ACM | grep -z '\\.go$' | xargs -0 golangci-lint run --enable-only dupl --new=false --max-issues-per-linter=0 --max-same-issues=0
"""

[tasks.bench]
description = "Run all benchmarks"
run = '''
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

output=$(go test -bench=. -benchmem -run='^$' -timeout=10m ./... 2>&1)

# Print non-benchmark lines (ok, PASS, etc.) to stderr
echo "$output" | grep -v '^Benchmark' >&2

# Format benchmark lines as a table with headers using column
bench_lines=$(echo "$output" | grep '^Benchmark' || true)
if [ -n "$bench_lines" ]; then
  {
    echo "BENCHMARK ITERS MS/OP NS/OP B/OP ALLOCS/OP"
    echo "--------- ----- ----- ----- ---- ---------"
    # Strip unit suffixes and add ms/op column (ns/op / 1000000)
    echo "$bench_lines" | sed 's/ ns\/op//g; s/ B\/op//g; s/ allocs\/op//g; s/ transcript_bytes//g' \
      | awk '{printf "%s %s %.2f %s %s %s\n", $1, $2, $3/1000000, $3, $4, $5}'
  } | column -t
fi
'''

name: E2E Tests

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

# Concurrency: only one E2E job runs at a time
concurrency:
  group: e2e-tests
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  e2e-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 40
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        agent: [claude, opencode, gemini]

    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - name: Setup mise
        uses: jdx/mise-action@v3

      - name: Install system dependencies
        run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y tmux

      - name: Build entire CLI
        run: go build -o /usr/local/bin/entire ./cmd/entire

      - name: Install agent CLI
        run: |
          case "${{ matrix.agent }}" in
            claude)   curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash ;;
            opencode) curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash ;;
            gemini)   npm install -g @google/gemini-cli ;;
          esac
          echo "$HOME/.local/bin" >> $GITHUB_PATH

      - name: Bootstrap agent
        env:
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          GEMINI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GEMINI_API_KEY }}
        run: go run ./e2e/bootstrap

      - name: Run E2E Tests
        env:
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
          GEMINI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GEMINI_API_KEY }}
          E2E_ENTIRE_BIN: /usr/local/bin/entire
        run: mise run test:e2e:${{ matrix.agent }}

      - name: Upload artifacts
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: e2e-artifacts-${{ matrix.agent }}
          path: e2e/artifacts/
          retention-days: 7

# Debug Entire CLI via E2E Artifacts

Diagnose Entire CLI bugs using captured artifacts from the E2E test suite. Artifacts are written to `e2e/artifacts/` locally or downloaded from CI via GitHub Actions.

## Inputs

The user provides either:
- **A test run directory:** `e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/` — triage all failures
- **A specific test directory:** `e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/{TestName}-{agent}/` — debug one test

## Artifact Layout

```
e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/
├── report.nocolor.txt          # Pass/fail/skip summary with error lines
├── test-events.json            # Raw Go test events (NDJSON)
├── entire-version.txt          # CLI version under test
└── {TestName}-{agent}/
    ├── PASS or FAIL            # Status marker
    ├── console.log             # Full operation transcript
    ├── git-log.txt             # git log --decorate --graph --all
    ├── git-tree.txt            # ls-tree HEAD + checkpoint branch
    ├── entire-logs/entire.log  # CLI structured JSON logs
    ├── checkpoint-metadata/    # Checkpoint + session metadata
    └── repo -> /tmp/...        # Symlink to preserved repo (E2E_KEEP_REPOS=1 only)
```

## Preserved Repo

When the test run was executed with `E2E_KEEP_REPOS=1`, each test's artifact directory contains a `repo` symlink pointing to the preserved temporary git repository. This is the actual repo the test operated on — you can inspect it directly.

**Navigate via the symlink** (e.g., `{artifact-dir}/repo/`) rather than resolving the `/tmp/...` path. The symlink lives inside the artifact directory so permissions and paths stay consistent.

The preserved repo contains:
- Full git history with all branches (main, `entire/checkpoints/v1`)
- The `.entire/` directory with CLI state, config, and raw logs
- The `.claude/` directory (if Claude Code was the agent)
- All files the agent created or modified, in their final state

This is the most powerful debugging tool — you can run `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, inspect `.entire/` internals, and see exactly what the CLI left behind.

## Debugging Workflow

### 1. Triage (if given a run directory)

Read `report.nocolor.txt` to identify failures and their error messages. Each entry shows the test name, agent, duration, and failure output with file:line references.

### 2. Read console.log (most important)

Full transcript of every operation:
- `> claude -p "..." ...` — agent prompts with stdout/stderr
- `> git add/commit/...` — git commands
- `> send: ...` — interactive session inputs

This tells you what happened chronologically.

### 3. Read test source code

Use the file:line from the report to find the test in `e2e/tests/`. Understand what the test expected to happen vs what console.log shows actually happened.

### 4. Diagnose the CLI behavior

Cross-reference console.log (what happened) with the test (what should have happened). Focus on CLI-level issues:

| Symptom | CLI Investigation |
|---------|-------------------|
| Checkpoint not created / timeout | Check `entire-logs/entire.log` for hook invocations, phase transitions, errors |
| Wrong checkpoint content | Check `git-tree.txt` for checkpoint branch files, `checkpoint-metadata/` for session info |
| Hooks didn't fire | Check `entire.log` for missing hook entries (session-start, user-prompt-submit, stop, post-commit) |
| Stash/unstash problems | Check `entire.log` for stash-related log lines, `git-log.txt` for commit ordering |
| Attribution issues | Check `checkpoint-metadata/` for `files_touched`, session metadata for attribution data |
| Strategy mismatch | Check `entire.log` for `strategy` field, verify auto-commit vs manual-commit behavior |

### 5. Deep dive files

- **entire-logs/entire.log**: Structured JSON logs — hook lifecycle, session phases (`active` → `idle` → `ended`), warnings, errors. Key fields: `component`, `hook`, `strategy`, `session_id`.
- **git-log.txt**: Commit graph showing main branch, `entire/checkpoints/v1`, checkpoint initialization.
- **git-tree.txt**: Files at HEAD vs checkpoint branch (separated by `--- entire/checkpoints/v1 ---`).
- **checkpoint-metadata/**: `metadata.json` has `checkpoint_id`, `strategy`, `files_touched`, `token_usage`, and `sessions` array. Session subdirs have per-session details.

### 6. Report findings

Identify whether the issue is in:
- **CLI hooks** (prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit)
- **Session management** (phase transitions, session tracking)
- **Checkpoint creation** (branch management, metadata writing)
- **Attribution** (file tracking, prompt correlation)
- **Strategy logic** (auto-commit vs manual-commit behavior)

Now I can see the issue with TestInteractiveContentOverlapRevertNewFile. Let me trace through what happened:

1. Session started, agent created `docs/red.md` (during the first Send)
2. The agent committed the file (line 10: prepare-commit-msg fired, checkpoint trailer added - `e8555fc755ff`)
3. Turn ended, session went ACTIVE → IDLE
4. But then the test replaces `docs/red.md` content and does `git add` + `git commit -m "Replace red.md content"`

The issue: The agent committed the file during its turn (line 10-14, prepare-commit-msg/commit-msg hooks fired). 

Looking at the timestamps more carefully, the post-commit hook actually fires after the turn-end hook is invoked but before the phase transitions to IDLE—so there's a window where the agent's commit is being processed while the turn is technically ending.

The real issue is that the agent itself committed the file with an Entire-Checkpoint trailer during its turn, but the test expects the user's subsequent commit (which overwrites the content) to have no trailer and not advance the checkpoint branch. The test flow shows the agent creating the file first, then the user replacing it, but the logs suggest the agent already committed it with the trailer before the user even got a chance to modify it. Looking at the timestamps more carefully, the prepare-commit-msg hook fired at 14:14:27.689 and turn-end happened at 14:14:27.859, which means OpenCode committed the file during its turn and the hook added the checkpoint trailer to that commit. Then the user's subsequent `git commit` created a second commit on top of it, but the test is checking HEAD for the trailer, which should be the user's commit without one. created a checkpoint with the Entire-Checkpoint trailer, which means the shadow branch got cleaned up. So when the user commits their replacement content, there's no agent content left to conflict with—the test's assumption that no checkpoint should be created doesn't hold because the agent already committed during its turn.

The real issue is that the user's commit shows the agent's checkpoint trailer in HEAD, which suggests either the user's commit never actually happened, or it happened but somehow inherited the trailer from the previous commit. Looking at the console output, I see the user's `git add` and `git commit` commands, but the test is still finding the agent's checkpoint ID on HEAD. This means the user's commit either didn't execute properly, or the post-commit hook is somehow carrying over the trailer to subsequent commits. Looking at the logs more carefully, there's no second prepare-commit-msg hook entry for the user's commit, which suggests it either didn't execute or failed silently. The user modified and staged the file, but the commit might not have actually gone through—maybe there was nothing new to commit, or the file state changed between the add and commit. The real issue is that OpenCode committed during its turn when the test expected it to just create the file without committing, which is why the agent's commit with the Entire-Checkpoint trailer ended up as HEAD instead of the user's commit. -deterministic agent behavior where OpenCode sometimes commits during a turn and sometimes doesn't. All three show `Token refresh failed: 400` in stderr — OpenCode can't authenticate. The agent never ran.

But the entire.log shows OpenCode committed the file during its turn (prepare-commit-msg fired at `:27.689`, adding trailer `e8555fc755ff`). The condensation ran, the checkpoint branch advanced, and the shadow branch was deleted — all before the user's replacement commit. The test then fails because it finds the agent's checkpoint trailer on HEAD and the checkpoint branch advanced "unexpectedly".

1. **OpenCode auth** — not related to our changes. Likely a stale token or API-side issue.
2. **Agent-committed-during-turn** — non-deterministic agent behavior. OpenCode sometimes commits the file itself when told to "create" it. The test was designed for agents that only write files without committing. This is pre-existing and not related to our branch.

None of the failures are related to the E2E infrastructure changes in this PR.

content.text:
There's no `[retry]` line. The stderr has `Error: Token refresh failed: 400` with ANSI escape codes. `detectStderrError` checks for `strings.HasPrefix(trimmed, "Error:")` — but the trimmed line starts with ANSI codes `[0m[91m[1mError:`, not bare `Error:`.

So the bug is: OpenCode exits 0, `detectStderrError` doesn't match because of ANSI escapes, `RunPrompt` returns `(out, nil)`, and the retry path (which requires `err != nil`) is never entered.

The fix is to strip ANSI codes in `detectStderrError`.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Gemini CLI configuration directory settings:

## Configuration Directory Location

Gemini CLI configuration files are stored in a dedicated `.gemini` directory within your home directory at `~/.gemini/`.

## GEMINI_CONFIG_DIR Environment Variable

The GEMINI_CONFIG_DIR environment variable is used to specify a custom path for the .gemini config directory. However, it's important to note that GEMINI_CONFIG_DIR has been requested and referenced in code, but platform-specific bugs and inconsistent behavior (particularly on Windows) have been reported, meaning environment-variable-based redirection may not be uniformly reliable on every platform or release.

## Alternative Configuration Directory Option

Instead of GEMINI_CONFIG_DIR, there's a more reliable environment variable: GEMINI_CLI_HOME specifies the root directory for Gemini CLI's user-level configuration and storage, which by default is the user's system home directory, and the CLI will create a .gemini folder inside this directory.

## Current Status

Currently, the Gemini CLI hardcodes the configuration directory to .gemini within the user's home directory, which limits flexibility for users who may wish to store configuration files in a different location. There has been a feature request (Issue #2815) to make the configuration directory configurable via environment variable.

## Search Results for OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR

Based on the search results, here's what I found about OpenCode's `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` environment variable:

### Overview
You can specify a custom config directory using the OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR environment variable. This directory will be searched for agents, commands, modes, and plugins just like the standard .opencode directory, and should follow the same structure.

### Configuration Structure
The .opencode and ~/.config/opencode directories use plural names for subdirectories: agents/, commands/, modes/, plugins/, skills/, tools/, and themes/.

### Loading Order and Precedence
Config sources are loaded in this order (later sources override earlier ones): Remote config (from .well-known/opencode) - organizational defaults · Global config (~/.config/opencode/opencode.json) - user preferences · Custom config (OPENCODE_CONFIG env var) - custom overrides · Project config (opencode.json in project) - project-specific settings

The custom directory is loaded after the global config and .opencode directories, so it can override their settings.

### Usage Example
You can use it like: export OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR=/path/to/my/config-directory opencode run "Hello world"

### Benefits
The OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR environment variable adds flexibility for power users, portable installations, or testing scenarios where a specific config location is needed regardless of the OS default.

## Custom Instructions and Rules

You can specify custom instruction files in your opencode.json or the global ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json. When opencode starts, it looks for rule files in this order: Local files by traversing up from the current directory (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md), Global file at ~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md, Claude Code file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (unless disabled).

## System Prompts for Agents

You can specify a custom system prompt file for an agent with the prompt config. The prompt file should contain instructions specific to the agent's purpose. This path is relative to where the config file is located. So this works for both the global OpenCode config and the project specific config.

Similarly, you can specify a custom system prompt file for a mode with the prompt config. The prompt file should contain instructions specific to the mode's purpose.

## Configuration Locations

The .opencode and ~/.config/opencode directories use plural names for subdirectories: agents/, commands/, modes/, plugins/, skills/, tools/, and themes/.

## Custom Commands

Custom commands are predefined prompts stored as Markdown files in one of three locations. Each .md file in these directories becomes a custom command. The file name (without extension) becomes the command ID.

# Debug Entire CLI via E2E Artifacts

Diagnose Entire CLI bugs using captured artifacts from the E2E test suite. Artifacts are written to `e2e/artifacts/` locally or downloaded from CI via GitHub Actions.

## Inputs

The user provides either:
- **A test run directory:** `e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/` — triage all failures
- **A specific test directory:** `e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/{TestName}-{agent}/` — debug one test

## Artifact Layout

```
e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/
├── report.nocolor.txt          # Pass/fail/skip summary with error lines
├── test-events.json            # Raw Go test events (NDJSON)
├── entire-version.txt          # CLI version under test
└── {TestName}-{agent}/
    ├── PASS or FAIL            # Status marker
    ├── console.log             # Full operation transcript
    ├── git-log.txt             # git log --decorate --graph --all
    ├── git-tree.txt            # ls-tree HEAD + checkpoint branch
    ├── entire-logs/entire.log  # CLI structured JSON logs
    ├── checkpoint-metadata/    # Checkpoint + session metadata
    └── repo -> /tmp/...        # Symlink to preserved repo (E2E_KEEP_REPOS=1 only)
```

## Preserved Repo

When the test run was executed with `E2E_KEEP_REPOS=1`, each test's artifact directory contains a `repo` symlink pointing to the preserved temporary git repository. This is the actual repo the test operated on — you can inspect it directly.

**Navigate via the symlink** (e.g., `{artifact-dir}/repo/`) rather than resolving the `/tmp/...` path. The symlink lives inside the artifact directory so permissions and paths stay consistent.

The preserved repo contains:
- Full git history with all branches (main, `entire/checkpoints/v1`)
- The `.entire/` directory with CLI state, config, and raw logs
- The `.claude/` directory (if Claude Code was the agent)
- All files the agent created or modified, in their final state

This is the most powerful debugging tool — you can run `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, inspect `.entire/` internals, and see exactly what the CLI left behind.

## Debugging Workflow

### 1. Triage (if given a run directory)

Read `report.nocolor.txt` to identify failures and their error messages. Each entry shows the test name, agent, duration, and failure output with file:line references.

### 2. Read console.log (most important)

Full transcript of every operation:
- `> claude -p "..." ...` — agent prompts with stdout/stderr
- `> git add/commit/...` — git commands
- `> send: ...` — interactive session inputs

This tells you what happened chronologically.

### 3. Read test source code

Use the file:line from the report to find the test in `e2e/tests/`. Understand what the test expected to happen vs what console.log shows actually happened.

### 4. Diagnose the CLI behavior

Cross-reference console.log (what happened) with the test (what should have happened). Focus on CLI-level issues:

| Symptom | CLI Investigation |
|---------|-------------------|
| Checkpoint not created / timeout | Check `entire-logs/entire.log` for hook invocations, phase transitions, errors |
| Wrong checkpoint content | Check `git-tree.txt` for checkpoint branch files, `checkpoint-metadata/` for session info |
| Hooks didn't fire | Check `entire.log` for missing hook entries (session-start, user-prompt-submit, stop, post-commit) |
| Stash/unstash problems | Check `entire.log` for stash-related log lines, `git-log.txt` for commit ordering |
| Attribution issues | Check `checkpoint-metadata/` for `files_touched`, session metadata for attribution data |
| Strategy mismatch | Check `entire.log` for `strategy` field, verify auto-commit vs manual-commit behavior |

### 5. Deep dive files

- **entire-logs/entire.log**: Structured JSON logs — hook lifecycle, session phases (`active` → `idle` → `ended`), warnings, errors. Key fields: `component`, `hook`, `strategy`, `session_id`.
- **git-log.txt**: Commit graph showing main branch, `entire/checkpoints/v1`, checkpoint initialization.
- **git-tree.txt**: Files at HEAD vs checkpoint branch (separated by `--- entire/checkpoints/v1 ---`).
- **checkpoint-metadata/**: `metadata.json` has `checkpoint_id`, `strategy`, `files_touched`, `token_usage`, and `sessions` array. Session subdirs have per-session details.

### 6. Report findings

Identify whether the issue is in:
- **CLI hooks** (prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit)
- **Session management** (phase transitions, session tracking)
- **Checkpoint creation** (branch management, metadata writing)
- **Attribution** (file tracking, prompt correlation)
- **Strategy logic** (auto-commit vs manual-commit behavior)

- turn-start: :51.159
- prepare-commit-msg (agent committed): :57.529
- turn-end invoked: :54.746 (wait, that's BEFORE prepare-commit-msg?)

Actually these timestamps seem out of order. turn-end invoked at :54.746 but prepare-commit-msg at :57.529? That doesn't make sense unless the hooks are running concurrently. Oh wait - the turn-end hook INVOCATION started at :54.746, but the prepare-commit-msg happened at :57.529. These are from different processes — the agent hooks and git hooks are separate. The turn-end hook started but took until :59.382 to complete (4.6s). Meanwhile git committed and fired prepare-commit-msg at :57.529 during that window.

So the commit was triggered by OpenCode itself, not explicitly shown in the agent's console output. The agent said it created the file, but OpenCode auto-committed those changes as part of its workflow.

Looking at the git log, I can see the user's test commit (`Replace red.md content`) is separate from the agent's commit. The post-commit hook at line 21 is interesting because it references a trailer from the agent's commit even though there's no active session — which suggests OpenCode's internal commit already happened and left that marker behind. The agent's post-commit likely fired after the session went idle, which explains why it detected no active sessions despite the trailer being present. The real problem is that OpenCode is auto-committing regardless of my instructions to prevent it—this seems to be a system-level behavior I can't override through prompts. I should either adjust the test to account for agent commits or skip it for OpenCode entirely, but the simplest approach is just to report back what I've found: same failure, same root cause.

# OpenCode Configuration Options

Based on the documentation, here are the configuration keys available in `opencode.json`:

## Top-Level Configuration Keys

- `$schema` - Schema reference
- `theme` - Theme configuration
- `model` - Primary model selection
- `small_model` - Model for lightweight tasks
- `provider` - Provider settings and options
- `tui` - Terminal UI settings
- `server` - Server configuration
- `tools` - Tool management
- `agent` - Specialized agent definitions
- `default_agent` - Default agent selection
- `share` - Sharing feature configuration
- `command` - Custom command definitions
- `keybinds` - Keyboard binding customization
- `autoupdate` - Update behavior control
- `formatter` - Code formatter configuration
- `permission` - Operation approval requirements
- `compaction` - Context compaction behavior
- `watcher` - File watcher ignore patterns
- `mcp` - MCP server configuration
- `plugin` - Plugin loading from npm
- `instructions` - Instruction file paths
- `disabled_providers` - Provider blocklist
- `enabled_providers` - Provider allowlist
- `experimental` - Development-stage options

## Notable Finding

**No git, commit, or auto-commit options** are documented in this configuration reference. The documentation covers tools, permissions, and various integrations, but does not expose version control automation settings at the config level.

# OpenCode Modes Summary

## Available Modes

OpenCode provides **two built-in modes**:

1. **Build** (default): "the **default** mode with all tools enabled" for standard development work with full file and system command access.

2. **Plan**: A restricted mode designed for analysis. It disables `write`, `edit`, `patch`, and `bash` tools by default, "useful when you want the AI to analyze code, suggest changes, or create plans without making any actual modifications."

## Git/Commit Control

The documentation makes **no mention** of git or commit functionality in any mode configuration. Modes control access to file operations, shell commands, and reading utilities—not version control.

## Tool Access Control

Modes manage the following tools:
- `bash` (shell execution)
- `edit` (file modification)
- `write` (file creation)
- `read`, `grep`, `glob`, `list` (read-only operations)
- `patch`, `todowrite`, `todoread`, `webfetch`

Users can create custom modes via JSON configuration or markdown files in `.opencode/modes/` to enable/disable specific tools for different workflows.

# Agent Configuration Information

## Agent Modes

OpenCode supports three agent modes:
- **Primary**: Main assistants you interact with directly (Build and Plan are built-in)
- **Subagent**: Specialized assistants invoked by primary agents or via @ mentions (General and Explore are built-in)
- **All**: Default when no mode specified

## Git Operations & Tool Restrictions

The documentation does **not** address git operation avoidance or auto-commit behavior. However, it extensively covers tool restrictions:

**Permission-Based Control**: Agents can restrict tool access through permissions set to `"ask"`, `"allow"`, or `"deny"`. Specific bash commands support glob patterns:

> "You can set permissions for specific bash commands... This can take a glob pattern."

**Example bash restrictions**:
```json
"bash": {
  "git *": "ask",
  "git status *": "allow"
}
```

**Tool Disabling**: Agents can disable specific tools entirely via the `tools` configuration, including write, edit, and bash operations.

**No Git-Specific Safeguards**: The documentation contains no built-in protections specifically preventing git push/commit operations—only general permission frameworks allowing per-command control.

## Key Configuration Options

- **Model override** per agent
- **Temperature** (0.0-1.0) for response creativity
- **Max steps** to limit agentic iterations
- **Prompt customization** via files
- **Task permissions** controlling subagent invocation
- **Color** for UI customization

# OpenCode Permissions Configuration Guide

## Core Permission Actions

OpenCode resolves permissions to three outcomes:
- `"allow"` — executes without approval
- `"ask"` — prompts user for confirmation
- `"deny"` — blocks the action

## Configuration Structure

Permissions use a hierarchical system with global settings overridable per-tool:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "*": "ask",
    "bash": "allow",
    "edit": "deny"
  }
}
```

Or apply uniformly: `"permission": "allow"`

## Available Permission Keys

**File Operations:**
- `read` — file access (matches file path)
- `edit` — all modifications including write, patch, multiedit
- `list` — directory listing
- `glob` — file globbing patterns
- `grep` — content search via regex

**Command & System:**
- `bash` — shell command execution
- `lsp` — language server protocol queries
- `task` — subagent launching
- `skill` — skill loading
- `webfetch` — URL fetching
- `websearch`, `codesearch` — search operations

**Special Guards:**
- `external_directory` — paths outside working directory
- `doom_loop` — repeated identical tool calls (triggers after 3 attempts)
- `todoread`, `todowrite` — todo list operations

## Granular Rule Syntax

Apply different actions based on input patterns:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "bash": {
      "*": "ask",
      "git *": "allow",
      "git commit *": "deny",
      "git push *": "deny"
    }
  }
}
```

**Matching Rules:**
- `*` matches zero or more characters
- `?` matches exactly one character
- Last matching rule wins
- Patterns are case-sensitive

## Path Matching Features

**Home Directory Expansion:**
- `~/projects/*` expands to user home
- `$HOME/projects/*` also supported
- Applied when writing patterns, not workspace behavior

**External Directory Access:**

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "external_directory": {
      "~/projects/personal/**": "allow"
    },
    "edit": {
      "~/projects/personal/**": "deny"
    }
  }
}
```

Paths outside the working directory require explicit `external_directory` allowance.

## Default Behavior

Unless configured:
- Most permissions default to `"allow"`
- `doom_loop` and `external_directory` default to `"ask"`
- `.env` files blocked by default; `.env.example` allowed

## Approval Workflow

When prompting ("ask" mode), users select:
- `once` — approve single request
- `always` — approve matching patterns for current session
- `reject` — deny request

## Agent-Level Overrides

Per-agent permissions override global config:

```json
{
  "permission": { "bash": { "*": "ask", "git *": "allow" } },
  "agent": {
    "review": {
      "permission": { "edit": "deny" }
    }
  }
}
```

Markdown agent config also supported via frontmatter.

# E2E Tests

End-to-end tests for the `entire` CLI against real agents (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode).

## Commands

```bash
mise run test:e2e TestFoo              # run filtered (or omit filter for all agents)
mise run test:e2e:claude TestFoo       # Claude Code only
mise run test:e2e:gemini TestFoo       # Gemini CLI only (sequential, avoids rate limits)
mise run test:e2e:opencode TestFoo     # OpenCode only
go build ./...                         # compile check (no agent CLI needed)
```

**Do NOT run E2E tests proactively.** They make real API calls that consume tokens and cost money. Only run when explicitly asked.

## Structure

```
e2e/
├── agents/       # Agent abstraction (Agent interface, tmux sessions, concurrency gates)
├── bootstrap/    # CI pre-test setup (auth config, warmup)
├── entire/       # `entire` CLI wrapper (enable, rewind, etc.)
├── exploratory/  # Experimental tests, not run by CI
├── tests/        # Blessed test files (run by CI)
└── testutil/     # Repo setup, assertions, artifact capture
```

## Key Patterns

- Every test uses `testutil.ForEachAgent` which runs it per registered agent with repo setup, concurrency gating, and timeout scaling.
- All operations go through `RepoState` (`s.RunPrompt`, `s.Git`) so they're logged to `console.log`.
- Use the `entire` package for CLI interactions, not raw `exec.Command`.
- Skip tests pending CLI fixes with `t.Skip("ENT-XXX: reason")`.

## Adding a New Agent

1. Create `agents/<name>.go` implementing the `Agent` interface.
2. Register it in `init()` with `Register(&YourAgent{})`.
3. Add a `Bootstrap()` method for any CI-specific setup (auth config, warmup).
4. Add a `RegisterGate("<name>", N)` call if concurrency needs limiting.
5. Add a `test:e2e:<name>` task in `mise.toml`.
6. Add the agent to `.github/workflows/e2e.yml` matrix and `e2e-isolated.yml` options.

## Environment Variables

| Variable | Description | Default |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| `E2E_AGENT` | Agent to test (`claude-code`, `gemini-cli`, `opencode`) | all registered |
| `E2E_ENTIRE_BIN` | Path to a pre-built `entire` binary | builds from source |
| `E2E_TIMEOUT` | Timeout per prompt | `2m` |
| `E2E_KEEP_REPOS` | Set to `1` to preserve temp repos after test | unset |
| `E2E_ARTIFACT_DIR` | Override artifact output directory | `e2e/artifacts/<timestamp>` |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Required for Claude Code | — |
| `GEMINI_API_KEY` | Required for Gemini CLI | — |

## Debugging Failures

Artifacts are captured to `e2e/artifacts/` on every run (git-log, git-tree, console.log, checkpoint metadata, entire logs). Set `E2E_KEEP_REPOS=1` to preserve the temp repo — a symlink appears in the artifact dir pointing to it.

Use the `debug-e2e` skill (`.claude/skills/debug-e2e/`) for a structured workflow when investigating failures.

### Reading artifacts

- `console.log` — full operation transcript including agent stdout/stderr
- `git-log.txt` — commit history at time of failure
- `git-tree.txt` — working tree state
- `entire-logs/` — internal CLI logs

### Fixing flaky tests

When a test passes on retry but failed once, the problem is usually agent non-determinism, not a CLI bug. Common patterns:

- **Agent asked for confirmation instead of acting**: The model output contains "Does this look right?" or "Should I proceed?". Fix: append "Do not ask for confirmation, just make the change." to the prompt.
- **Agent wrote to wrong path or created extra files**: Fix: be more explicit about exact file paths and what _not_ to do.
- **Agent committed when it shouldn't have**: Fix: add "Do not commit" to the prompt.
- **Checkpoint wait timeout**: `WaitForCheckpoint` or `WaitForCheckpointAdvanceFrom` exceeded deadline. Fix: increase the timeout argument.

To diagnose: read `console.log` in the failing test's artifact directory. Compare what the agent actually did vs what the test expected.

## CI Workflows

- **`.github/workflows/e2e.yml`** — Runs full suite on push to main. Matrix: `[claude, opencode, gemini]`.
- **`.github/workflows/e2e-isolated.yml`** — Manual dispatch for debugging a single test. Inputs: agent + test name filter.

Both workflows run `go run ./e2e/bootstrap` before tests to handle agent-specific CI setup (auth config, warmup).
# Exploratory E2E Tests

Tests in this directory are **not run by CI**. They exist for:

- Validating bug fixes before the fix is merged (reference the Linear issue)
- Prototyping new test scenarios before promoting to `tests/`
- Reproducing reported issues

## Running

    go test -tags=e2e -count=1 -timeout=30m ./exploratory/...

## Promoting to blessed

# GitHub Issue #1467: Disabling Git Commands in OpenCode

## The Problem

User bczsalba reported that OpenCode inadvertently executes git commands when certain words are mentioned. The core complaint centers on accidental data loss:

> "whenever you utter the word 'undo' there is roughly a 50% chance that you get a context-aware undo"

This creates a dangerous situation where uncommitted work can be permanently lost with minimal warning. The reporter states they have no use case for OpenCode running git operations and wanted a configuration option to disable this functionality entirely.

## Proposed Solutions

The issue reporter considered but rejected a workaround involving shell-level trickery, deeming it unreliable. They explicitly requested:

- A proper configuration setting to wholesale disable git command execution
- An official, maintainable solution rather than environmental hacks

## Official Response

The issue was **closed as COMPLETED** on August 6, 2025. Resolution came through:

- **Pull Request #1627** ("permissions disallow support") was merged
- Assignee thdxr managed the implementation
- The solution addressed the underlying permissions system to prevent unwanted git operations

No detailed explanation of the technical implementation was visible in the provided content.

content.content:
# GitHub Issue #3239 Summary: Auto-Commit Problem in OpenCode

## Problem Reported
User George complained that an AI agent was automatically committing code changes despite explicit instructions not to do so. When asked to add these restrictions to guidelines, the agent ironically auto-committed the very changes documenting the prohibition against auto-committing.

## Key Issue
The agent failed to respect written instructions: "NEVER AUTO COMMIT and NEVER ASSUME A NEW IMPLEMENTATION JUST WORKS!" Even after agreeing to follow this rule and updating documentation, the agent immediately violated it by auto-committing the guideline updates.

## Solutions Suggested

**Permission-Based Control (Recommended):**
A collaborator (Aiden Cline) provided this configuration for `opencode.json`:

```json
"permission": {
  "bash": {
    "rm *": "ask",
    "git push *": "ask",
    "git commit *": "ask"
  }
}
```

This approach enforces deterministic rules rather than relying on LLM instruction-following.

**Additional Workaround:**
User Oliver reported success after restarting the application following configuration changes, suggesting the tool requires restart for permission updates to take effect.

## Official Response
The maintainer confirmed that permission-based restrictions are the intended safeguard mechanism and acknowledged that configuration hot-reloading isn't yet implemented—users must restart after modifying permissions.

## Key Findings

OpenCode uses a permission system in opencode.json where you can configure bash command permissions, including setting "git commit *" to "deny". 

### Permission Configuration

Setting permissions to "deny" is the strictest option, blocking the LLM from running that command or command pattern. The opencode.json configuration allows you to set specific permissions for different bash commands like "git *" to "allow", "git commit *" to "deny", and "git push *" to "deny".

### How Permissions Work

You can override permissions per agent, and agent permissions are merged with the global config, with agent rules taking precedence. Rules are evaluated by pattern match with the last matching rule winning, and a common pattern is to put the catch-all "*" rule first with more specific rules after it.

### Example Configuration

A typical opencode.json configuration might look like a schema with a permission object containing bash settings, where you can deny git commit operations at the global level and override it at the agent level.

The documentation demonstrates that OpenCode's permission system provides granular control over bash commands, allowing administrators to restrict sensitive git operations like commits and pushes while allowing safer operations like status checks.

# OpenCode Built-in Tools

Based on the documentation, OpenCode provides **14 built-in tools**. There is **no dedicated git tool**—git commands run through the `bash` tool.

## Complete Built-in Tools List

1. **bash** - "Execute shell commands in your project environment," including git operations
2. **edit** - Modify files using exact string replacements
3. **write** - Create new files or overwrite existing ones
4. **read** - "Read file contents from your codebase"
5. **grep** - "Search file contents using regular expressions"
6. **glob** - "Find files by pattern matching"
7. **list** - "List files and directories in a given path"
8. **lsp** - Interact with LSP servers for code intelligence (experimental)
9. **patch** - "Apply patches to files"
10. **skill** - Load skill files and return their content
11. **todowrite** - "Manage todo lists during coding sessions"
12. **todoread** - Read existing todo lists
13. **webfetch** - "Fetch and read web pages"
14. **websearch** - Perform web searches using Exa AI
15. **question** - "Ask the user questions during execution"

All tools are enabled by default but can be controlled through permission settings in `opencode.json` using `allow`, `deny`, or `ask` values.

# OpenCode CLI Flags & Environment Variables

## Git-Related Flags

The documentation contains **no explicit git, commit, auto-commit, or non-interactive mode flags** in the traditional sense. However, the following flags affect automated behavior:

### Relevant for Automation:
- `--share`: "Share the session" (available with `run` command)
- `--continue` / `-c`: "Continue the last session"
- `--fork`: "Fork the session when continuing"
- `--format`: Supports `json` output for programmatic use

## Environment Variables (Git/Automation-Related)

**No dedicated git configuration variables exist.** However, these affect behavior:

- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATE`: "Disable automatic update checks"
- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_PRUNE`: "Disable pruning of old data"
- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOCOMPACT`: "Disable automatic context compaction"
- `OPENCODE_FAKE_VCS`: "Fake VCS provider for testing purposes"

## Non-Interactive Usage

The `run` command enables non-interactive operation: "Run opencode in non-interactive mode by passing a prompt directly." This accepts piped input and returns formatted or JSON output via the `--format` flag.

**Note:** OpenCode documentation doesn't expose git commit automation or direct VCS write operations through CLI flags—it focuses on code analysis and interactive assistance rather than automated commits.

content.text:
Here is a comprehensive summary of my findings:

---

## OpenCode CLI: Auto-Commit / Auto-Git Configuration Options

### 1. Does OpenCode have a setting to prevent automatic git commands?

**Yes.** OpenCode does not have a single toggle to disable "auto-commit," but it provides a granular **permissions system** that can block, prompt, or allow specific bash commands -- including all git operations. Since OpenCode has **no dedicated git tool** (all git operations run through the `bash` tool), controlling bash permissions is the mechanism for controlling git behavior.

The recommended configuration in `opencode.json`:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "bash": {
      "*": "allow",
      "git commit *": "deny",
      "git push *": "deny"
    }
  }
}
```

The three permission actions are:
- **`"allow"`** -- executes without approval
- **`"ask"`** -- prompts the user for confirmation before executing
- **`"deny"`** -- blocks the action entirely

To disable ALL git operations:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "bash": {
      "*": "allow",
      "git *": "deny",
      "git status *": "allow",
      "git diff *": "allow",
      "git log *": "allow"
    }
  }
}
```

The last matching rule wins, so you can deny `git *` broadly and then re-allow safe read-only commands.

### 2. Is there an `opencode.json` config option or environment variable?

**Config file: Yes. Environment variable: No.**

- **`opencode.json`** in the project root (highest precedence) or `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (global) supports the `permission` key with nested bash command patterns as shown above.
- There is **no environment variable** like `OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOCOMMIT`. The environment variables that exist (`OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATE`, `OPENCODE_DISABLE_PRUNE`, `OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOCOMPACT`) are unrelated to git.

**Important note about the default behavior:** OpenCode's built-in bash tool system prompt (in `bash.txt`) contains instructions telling the LLM to format git commits with a co-author line (`Co-Authored-By: opencode <noreply@opencode.ai>`) and a "Generated with opencode" footer. This means the LLM is *instructed* to commit in a certain style, but the actual auto-commit behavior is driven by the LLM deciding to run `git commit` via the bash tool. It is not a deterministic, built-in auto-commit feature -- it is an emergent behavior from the system prompt instructions.

This is why using **permissions** (which are deterministic and enforced before tool execution) is the reliable way to control this, rather than relying on rules/instructions (which the LLM may ignore, as documented in [Issue #3239](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/3239)).

### 3. Does OpenCode have "modes" or "agent" configurations that control auto-commit?

**Modes:** OpenCode has two built-in modes:
- **Build** (default) -- all tools enabled, including bash (and thus git)
- **Plan** -- disables `write`, `edit`, `patch`, and `bash` tools entirely. Since git runs through bash, Plan mode effectively prevents all git operations, but it also prevents all shell commands.

You can create **custom modes** (in `.opencode/modes/`) that selectively disable the bash tool, but this is a blunt instrument since it blocks all shell commands, not just git.

**Agents:** Agent-level permission overrides are supported:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "bash": {
      "git *": "allow"
    }
  },
  "agent": {
    "review": {
      "permission": {
        "bash": {
          "git *": "deny"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Agent permissions merge with and override global permissions, so you can have one agent that can commit and another that cannot.

### Summary Table

| Mechanism | Granularity | Reliability | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `permission.bash` with `"deny"` | Per-command pattern | Deterministic | Recommended approach |
| `permission.bash` with `"ask"` | Per-command pattern | Deterministic | Prompts before each git command |
| Rules/instructions ("never commit") | LLM instruction | Unreliable | LLM may ignore; documented in issues |
| Plan mode | All bash disabled | Deterministic | Too broad; blocks all shell commands |
| Agent-level permissions | Per-agent | Deterministic | Useful for multi-agent setups |

### Key Caveat

After changing `opencode.json` permissions, OpenCode **requires a restart** -- hot-reloading of permission config is not supported (confirmed by maintainers in [Issue #3239](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/3239)).

content.text:
Here is a comprehensive summary of my findings:

---

## OpenCode CLI: Auto-Commit / Auto-Git Configuration Options

### 1. Does OpenCode have a setting to prevent automatic git commands?

**Yes.** OpenCode does not have a single toggle to disable "auto-commit," but it provides a granular **permissions system** that can block, prompt, or allow specific bash commands -- including all git operations. Since OpenCode has **no dedicated git tool** (all git operations run through the `bash` tool), controlling bash permissions is the mechanism for controlling git behavior.

The recommended configuration in `opencode.json`:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "bash": {
      "*": "allow",
      "git commit *": "deny",
      "git push *": "deny"
    }
  }
}
```

The three permission actions are:
- **`"allow"`** -- executes without approval
- **`"ask"`** -- prompts the user for confirmation before executing
- **`"deny"`** -- blocks the action entirely

To disable ALL git operations:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "bash": {
      "*": "allow",
      "git *": "deny",
      "git status *": "allow",
      "git diff *": "allow",
      "git log *": "allow"
    }
  }
}
```

The last matching rule wins, so you can deny `git *` broadly and then re-allow safe read-only commands.

### 2. Is there an `opencode.json` config option or environment variable?

**Config file: Yes. Environment variable: No.**

- **`opencode.json`** in the project root (highest precedence) or `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (global) supports the `permission` key with nested bash command patterns as shown above.
- There is **no environment variable** like `OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOCOMMIT`. The environment variables that exist (`OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATE`, `OPENCODE_DISABLE_PRUNE`, `OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOCOMPACT`) are unrelated to git.

**Important note about the default behavior:** OpenCode's built-in bash tool system prompt (in `bash.txt`) contains instructions telling the LLM to format git commits with a co-author line (`Co-Authored-By: opencode <noreply@opencode.ai>`) and a "Generated with opencode" footer. This means the LLM is *instructed* to commit in a certain style, but the actual auto-commit behavior is driven by the LLM deciding to run `git commit` via the bash tool. It is not a deterministic, built-in auto-commit feature -- it is an emergent behavior from the system prompt instructions.

This is why using **permissions** (which are deterministic and enforced before tool execution) is the reliable way to control this, rather than relying on rules/instructions (which the LLM may ignore, as documented in [Issue #3239](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/3239)).

### 3. Does OpenCode have "modes" or "agent" configurations that control auto-commit?

**Modes:** OpenCode has two built-in modes:
- **Build** (default) -- all tools enabled, including bash (and thus git)
- **Plan** -- disables `write`, `edit`, `patch`, and `bash` tools entirely. Since git runs through bash, Plan mode effectively prevents all git operations, but it also prevents all shell commands.

You can create **custom modes** (in `.opencode/modes/`) that selectively disable the bash tool, but this is a blunt instrument since it blocks all shell commands, not just git.

**Agents:** Agent-level permission overrides are supported:

```json
{
  "permission": {
    "bash": {
      "git *": "allow"
    }
  },
  "agent": {
    "review": {
      "permission": {
        "bash": {
          "git *": "deny"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Agent permissions merge with and override global permissions, so you can have one agent that can commit and another that cannot.

### Summary Table

| Mechanism | Granularity | Reliability | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `permission.bash` with `"deny"` | Per-command pattern | Deterministic | Recommended approach |
| `permission.bash` with `"ask"` | Per-command pattern | Deterministic | Prompts before each git command |
| Rules/instructions ("never commit") | LLM instruction | Unreliable | LLM may ignore; documented in issues |
| Plan mode | All bash disabled | Deterministic | Too broad; blocks all shell commands |
| Agent-level permissions | Per-agent | Deterministic | Useful for multi-agent setups |

### Key Caveat

After changing `opencode.json` permissions, OpenCode **requires a restart** -- hot-reloading of permission config is not supported (confirmed by maintainers in [Issue #3239](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/3239)).

# Debug Entire CLI via E2E Artifacts

Diagnose Entire CLI bugs using captured artifacts from the E2E test suite. Artifacts are written to `e2e/artifacts/` locally or downloaded from CI via GitHub Actions.

## Inputs

The user provides either:
- **A test run directory:** `e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/` — triage all failures
- **A specific test directory:** `e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/{TestName}-{agent}/` — debug one test

## Artifact Layout

```
e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/
├── report.nocolor.txt          # Pass/fail/skip summary with error lines
├── test-events.json            # Raw Go test events (NDJSON)
├── entire-version.txt          # CLI version under test
└── {TestName}-{agent}/
    ├── PASS or FAIL            # Status marker
    ├── console.log             # Full operation transcript
    ├── git-log.txt             # git log --decorate --graph --all
    ├── git-tree.txt            # ls-tree HEAD + checkpoint branch
    ├── entire-logs/entire.log  # CLI structured JSON logs
    ├── checkpoint-metadata/    # Checkpoint + session metadata
    └── repo -> /tmp/...        # Symlink to preserved repo (E2E_KEEP_REPOS=1 only)
```

## Preserved Repo

When the test run was executed with `E2E_KEEP_REPOS=1`, each test's artifact directory contains a `repo` symlink pointing to the preserved temporary git repository. This is the actual repo the test operated on — you can inspect it directly.

**Navigate via the symlink** (e.g., `{artifact-dir}/repo/`) rather than resolving the `/tmp/...` path. The symlink lives inside the artifact directory so permissions and paths stay consistent.

The preserved repo contains:
- Full git history with all branches (main, `entire/checkpoints/v1`)
- The `.entire/` directory with CLI state, config, and raw logs
- The `.claude/` directory (if Claude Code was the agent)
- All files the agent created or modified, in their final state

This is the most powerful debugging tool — you can run `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, inspect `.entire/` internals, and see exactly what the CLI left behind.

## Debugging Workflow

### 1. Triage (if given a run directory)

Read `report.nocolor.txt` to identify failures and their error messages. Each entry shows the test name, agent, duration, and failure output with file:line references.

### 2. Read console.log (most important)

Full transcript of every operation:
- `> claude -p "..." ...` — agent prompts with stdout/stderr
- `> git add/commit/...` — git commands
- `> send: ...` — interactive session inputs

This tells you what happened chronologically.

### 3. Read test source code

Use the file:line from the report to find the test in `e2e/tests/`. Understand what the test expected to happen vs what console.log shows actually happened.

### 4. Diagnose the CLI behavior

Cross-reference console.log (what happened) with the test (what should have happened). Focus on CLI-level issues:

| Symptom | CLI Investigation |
|---------|-------------------|
| Checkpoint not created / timeout | Check `entire-logs/entire.log` for hook invocations, phase transitions, errors |
| Wrong checkpoint content | Check `git-tree.txt` for checkpoint branch files, `checkpoint-metadata/` for session info |
| Hooks didn't fire | Check `entire.log` for missing hook entries (session-start, user-prompt-submit, stop, post-commit) |
| Stash/unstash problems | Check `entire.log` for stash-related log lines, `git-log.txt` for commit ordering |
| Attribution issues | Check `checkpoint-metadata/` for `files_touched`, session metadata for attribution data |
| Strategy mismatch | Check `entire.log` for `strategy` field, verify auto-commit vs manual-commit behavior |

### 5. Deep dive files

- **entire-logs/entire.log**: Structured JSON logs — hook lifecycle, session phases (`active` → `idle` → `ended`), warnings, errors. Key fields: `component`, `hook`, `strategy`, `session_id`.
- **git-log.txt**: Commit graph showing main branch, `entire/checkpoints/v1`, checkpoint initialization.
- **git-tree.txt**: Files at HEAD vs checkpoint branch (separated by `--- entire/checkpoints/v1 ---`).
- **checkpoint-metadata/**: `metadata.json` has `checkpoint_id`, `strategy`, `files_touched`, `token_usage`, and `sessions` array. Session subdirs have per-session details.

### 6. Report findings

# Debug Entire CLI via E2E Artifacts

Diagnose Entire CLI bugs using captured artifacts from the E2E test suite. Artifacts are written to `e2e/artifacts/` locally or downloaded from CI via GitHub Actions.

## Inputs

The user provides either:
- **A test run directory:** `e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/` — triage all failures
- **A specific test directory:** `e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/{TestName}-{agent}/` — debug one test

## Artifact Layout

```
e2e/artifacts/{timestamp}/
├── report.nocolor.txt          # Pass/fail/skip summary with error lines
├── test-events.json            # Raw Go test events (NDJSON)
├── entire-version.txt          # CLI version under test
└── {TestName}-{agent}/
    ├── PASS or FAIL            # Status marker
    ├── console.log             # Full operation transcript
    ├── git-log.txt             # git log --decorate --graph --all
    ├── git-tree.txt            # ls-tree HEAD + checkpoint branch
    ├── entire-logs/entire.log  # CLI structured JSON logs
    ├── checkpoint-metadata/    # Checkpoint + session metadata
    └── repo -> /tmp/...        # Symlink to preserved repo (E2E_KEEP_REPOS=1 only)
```

## Preserved Repo

When the test run was executed with `E2E_KEEP_REPOS=1`, each test's artifact directory contains a `repo` symlink pointing to the preserved temporary git repository. This is the actual repo the test operated on — you can inspect it directly.

**Navigate via the symlink** (e.g., `{artifact-dir}/repo/`) rather than resolving the `/tmp/...` path. The symlink lives inside the artifact directory so permissions and paths stay consistent.

The preserved repo contains:
- Full git history with all branches (main, `entire/checkpoints/v1`)
- The `.entire/` directory with CLI state, config, and raw logs
- The `.claude/` directory (if Claude Code was the agent)
- All files the agent created or modified, in their final state

This is the most powerful debugging tool — you can run `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, inspect `.entire/` internals, and see exactly what the CLI left behind.

## Debugging Workflow

### 1. Triage (if given a run directory)

Read `report.nocolor.txt` to identify failures and their error messages. Each entry shows the test name, agent, duration, and failure output with file:line references.

### 2. Read console.log (most important)

Full transcript of every operation:
- `> claude -p "..." ...` — agent prompts with stdout/stderr
- `> git add/commit/...` — git commands
- `> send: ...` — interactive session inputs

This tells you what happened chronologically.

### 3. Read test source code

Use the file:line from the report to find the test in `e2e/tests/`. Understand what the test expected to happen vs what console.log shows actually happened.

### 4. Diagnose the CLI behavior

Cross-reference console.log (what happened) with the test (what should have happened). Focus on CLI-level issues:

| Symptom | CLI Investigation |
|---------|-------------------|
| Checkpoint not created / timeout | Check `entire-logs/entire.log` for hook invocations, phase transitions, errors |
| Wrong checkpoint content | Check `git-tree.txt` for checkpoint branch files, `checkpoint-metadata/` for session info |
| Hooks didn't fire | Check `entire.log` for missing hook entries (session-start, user-prompt-submit, stop, post-commit) |
| Stash/unstash problems | Check `entire.log` for stash-related log lines, `git-log.txt` for commit ordering |
| Attribution issues | Check `checkpoint-metadata/` for `files_touched`, session metadata for attribution data |
| Strategy mismatch | Check `entire.log` for `strategy` field, verify auto-commit vs manual-commit behavior |

### 5. Deep dive files

- **entire-logs/entire.log**: Structured JSON logs — hook lifecycle, session phases (`active` → `idle` → `ended`), warnings, errors. Key fields: `component`, `hook`, `strategy`, `session_id`.
- **git-log.txt**: Commit graph showing main branch, `entire/checkpoints/v1`, checkpoint initialization.
- **git-tree.txt**: Files at HEAD vs checkpoint branch (separated by `--- entire/checkpoints/v1 ---`).
- **checkpoint-metadata/**: `metadata.json` has `checkpoint_id`, `strategy`, `files_touched`, `token_usage`, and `sessions` array. Session subdirs have per-session details.

### 6. Report findings

Identify whether the issue is in:
- **CLI hooks** (prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit)
- **Session management** (phase transitions, session tracking)
- **Checkpoint creation** (branch management, metadata writing)
- **Attribution** (file tracking, prompt correlation)
- **Strategy logic** (auto-commit vs manual-commit behavior)

The 450s tests are hitting the overall test timeout, likely due to Gemini's 2.5x slowdown combined with retry backoff. The user's complaint makes sense—5 retries with exponential backoff wastes 62 seconds before failing anyway, and slow tests are getting pushed over the timeout limit by the retry mechanism itself.

Looking at the actual numbers, these "signal: killed" tests at 300-450s are just hitting the per-test timeout (2 minutes × 2.5 multiplier = 300s), not 500 errors. The real issue is whether we're running too many concurrent Gemini tests—the gate was set to 2, but I need to check if the `E2E_CONCURRENT_TEST_LIMIT` change is actually active in the workflow.

For local runs without that environment variable set, it defaults to 2 anyway. But looking at the test durations—some taking 200-450s, one passing at 427s—it's clear the Gemini API itself is just slow and flaky. The 500s are likely their infrastructure being unreliable, not something we're doing wrong. The question becomes whether retrying with exponential backoff actually helps or just compounds the problem.

If it's a sustained outage, we're wasting time with 5 retries and 62s of delay. If it's transient, retries save us. Maybe capping the max backoff or dropping to 3 attempts would be smarter, though the emoji reaction suggests we might be overthinking this. Let me check whether running concurrent tests is actually overwhelming their API and triggering these 500s.

1. **TestModifyExistingTrackedFile** (89.9s) — 5/5 retries exhausted on Gemini 500s. That's 2+4+8+16+32 = 62s of just backoff. The API was down for the entire duration.

2. **TestRewindMultipleFiles, TestSingleSessionSubagentCommitInTurn, TestSubagentCommitFlow** (300-450s) — `signal: killed`. Hit the per-test timeout. These are Gemini being slow, not 500s.

3. **TestModifiedFileAlwaysGetsCheckpoint** — shadow branch not cleaned up (different issue, not API related).

The 500s are Gemini's API being flaky — we can't fix that. But we're making it worse: **all tests are hammering Gemini concurrently with the gate at 2**, and when tests retry they add more load. The 5-retry exponential backoff turns a quick failure into a 90s test.

I think the backoff is working against us here. If Gemini returns 500, retrying 5 times won't help during a sustained outage — it just delays the inevitable and eats into the overall timeout budget. Maybe cap it at 2-3 retries with shorter delays?

The "Incomplete JSON segment" errors suggest streaming responses are getting cut short, while the INTERNAL 500s are actual server errors, and both are clustering around similar timestamps in the same run, pointing to periods of API instability rather than test-specific issues.

Looking at the error timestamps across our runs today - 15-13-03 had 3 Gemini 500s, 15-19-58 had 1, and 15-34-32 had 2 - I'm trying to see if these failures cluster together in time, which would indicate an outage window rather than isolated incidents. The user's asking me to look at patterns across all our Gemini runs, so I need to map out when these failures occurred relative to each other.

The "Incomplete JSON segment at the end" errors are particularly telling - that's a streaming issue where the response got cut off mid-stream. This could point to API instability, network problems, rate limiting, or the fact that we're using `gemini-3-flash-preview`, which is a preview model and might be less stable. Let me check what model we're actually using in the Gemini agent code.

content.text:
OK, looking at the actual errors across runs. The 500s are two types:

1. **`Incomplete JSON segment at the end`** — streaming response cut mid-stream
2. **`INTERNAL` 500** — generic server error

In TestPartialStaging, the 4 attempts hit at `:36:02`, `:36:10`, `:36:19`, `:36:28` — all within 26 seconds. Alternating between both error types. It's a sustained Gemini outage window, not individual request failures.

The shadow branch failures (TestModifyExistingTrackedFile) are a different issue — Gemini created extra files (`config_test.go`, `go.mod`) that weren't committed. Same over-eager agent behavior as OpenCode but different: Gemini writes tests and initializes modules. The carry-forward correctly tracks the uncommitted files.

**Pattern across runs**: the 500s hit random tests — whichever test happens to run during a Gemini API hiccup. It's not test-specific. And we're using `gemini-3-flash-preview` — a **preview** model, which may be less stable than GA.

Not much we can do about Gemini's API stability. The retries are the right mitigation. The shadow branch failures are the same agent over-eagerness problem — worth a separate look.

The user is asking about the shadow branch failures — the "shadow branches should be cleaned up after commit" errors that keep recurring with Gemini. Let me think about what's happening.

The pattern: Gemini (and sometimes OpenCode) creates extra files beyond what was asked (test files, go.mod, etc.). These extra files are tracked by the session but not committed by the test's `git add`/`git commit` (which only stages the expected files). So the carry-forward logic correctly creates a new shadow branch for the uncommitted agent-touched files.

This is the same root cause as the original failures from the user's CLAUDE.md leaking TDD instructions — except now it's the agents' own system prompts encouraging them to write tests, initialize modules, etc.


I'm looking at the affected tests and seeing the same issue across the board: Gemini keeps generating extra files like test files and module configs that don't get staged, leaving uncommitted changes that trigger the shadow branch cleanup logic. The real question is whether to tighten the prompts to prevent over-creation, stage everything the agent touches, or accept this behavior and adjust how we validate it.

content.text:
Same pattern both times:

1. **TestRapidSequentialCommits**: Gemini committed 3 files across 3 commits. The last commit (green.md) has shadow branch `entire/1e29f84-e3b0c4` with "carry forward: uncommitted session files". Something was left over that wasn't committed.

2. **TestModifyExistingTrackedFile**: Asked to modify `src/config.go`, Gemini also created `src/config_test.go` and `go.mod`. The test only does `git add src/config.go` — the extra files remain uncommitted, so carry-forward keeps the shadow branch.

It's the same root cause as the original CLAUDE.md leakage but from the agents' own system prompts. Two approaches:

1. **Fix the tests** — use `git add .` instead of staging specific files, so agent extras get committed too
2. **Fix the assertions** — only assert no shadow branches when we know the agent didn't create extras (fragile)
3. **Fix the prompts** — tell agents not to create extra files (unreliable, as we've seen)

Option 1 seems cleanest — the tests care about the CLI's checkpoint behavior, not which exact files the agent creates. Staging everything matches what a real user would do. Want me to go that route?

1→//go:build e2e
     2→
     3→package tests
     4→
     5→import (
     6→	"context"
     7→	"testing"
     8→	"time"
     9→
    10→	"github.com/entireio/cli/e2e/testutil"
    11→)
    12→
    13→// TestCheckpointMetadataDeepValidation runs deep validation on checkpoint metadata
    14→// including transcript JSONL, content hash, and prompt content.
    15→func TestCheckpointMetadataDeepValidation(t *testing.T) {
    16→	testutil.ForEachAgent(t, 2*time.Minute, func(t *testing.T, s *testutil.RepoState, ctx context.Context) {
    17→		prompt := "Create a file called validated.go with content 'package main; func Validated() {}'. " +
    18→			"Create only this file. Do not commit. " +
    19→			"Do not ask for confirmation, just make the change."
    20→
    21→		_, err := s.RunPrompt(t, ctx, prompt)
    22→		if err != nil {
    23→			t.Fatalf("agent failed: %v", err)
    24→		}
    25→
    26→		testutil.AssertFileExists(t, s.Dir, "validated.go")
    27→
    28→		s.Git(t, "add", "validated.go")
    29→		s.Git(t, "commit", "-m", "Add validated.go")
    30→		testutil.WaitForCheckpoint(t, s, 15*time.Second)
    31→
    32→		cpID := testutil.AssertHasCheckpointTrailer(t, s.Dir, "HEAD")
    33→		testutil.ValidateCheckpointDeep(t, s.Dir, testutil.DeepCheckpointValidation{
    34→			CheckpointID: cpID,
    35→			Strategy:     "manual-commit",
    36→			FilesTouched: []string{"validated.go"},
    37→		})
    38→		testutil.AssertNoShadowBranches(t, s.Dir)
    39→	})
    40→}
    41→

1→//go:build e2e
     2→
     3→package tests
     4→
     5→import (
     6→	"context"
     7→	"os"
     8→	"path/filepath"
     9→	"testing"
    10→	"time"
    11→
    12→	"github.com/entireio/cli/e2e/testutil"
    13→	"github.com/stretchr/testify/assert"
    14→	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
    15→)
    16→
    17→// TestDeletedFilesCommitDeletion tests that deleting a file that was tracked
    18→// in the session gets handled properly when committed via git rm.
    19→func TestDeletedFilesCommitDeletion(t *testing.T) {
    20→	testutil.ForEachAgent(t, 3*time.Minute, func(t *testing.T, s *testutil.RepoState, ctx context.Context) {
    21→		require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(
    22→			filepath.Join(s.Dir, "to_delete.go"),
    23→			[]byte("package main\n\nfunc ToDelete() {}\n"), 0o644))
    24→		s.Git(t, "add", "to_delete.go")
    25→		s.Git(t, "commit", "--no-verify", "-m", "Add to_delete.go")
    26→
    27→		_, err := s.RunPrompt(t, ctx,
    28→			"Do two things: (1) Delete the file to_delete.go using rm. "+
    29→				"(2) Create a new file replacement.go with content 'package main; func Replacement() {}'. "+
    30→				"Do both tasks. Do not commit. "+
    31→				"Do not ask for confirmation, just make the changes.")
    32→		if err != nil {
    33→			t.Fatalf("agent failed: %v", err)
    34→		}
    35→
    36→		assert.NoFileExists(t, filepath.Join(s.Dir, "to_delete.go"))
    37→		testutil.AssertFileExists(t, s.Dir, "replacement.go")
    38→
    39→		s.Git(t, "add", "replacement.go")
    40→		s.Git(t, "commit", "-m", "Add replacement")
    41→		testutil.WaitForCheckpoint(t, s, 15*time.Second)
    42→		cpID1 := testutil.AssertHasCheckpointTrailer(t, s.Dir, "HEAD")
    43→		testutil.AssertCheckpointExists(t, s.Dir, cpID1)
    44→
    45→		cpBranchAfterFirst := testutil.GitOutput(t, s.Dir, "rev-parse", "entire/checkpoints/v1")
    46→
    47→		s.Git(t, "rm", "to_delete.go")
    48→		s.Git(t, "commit", "-m", "Remove to_delete.go")
    49→
    50→		time.Sleep(5 * time.Second)
    51→		cpBranchAfterDeletion := testutil.GitOutput(t, s.Dir, "rev-parse", "entire/checkpoints/v1")
    52→		if cpBranchAfterDeletion != cpBranchAfterFirst {
    53→			cpID2 := testutil.AssertHasCheckpointTrailer(t, s.Dir, "HEAD")
    54→			assert.NotEqual(t, cpID1, cpID2, "checkpoint IDs should be distinct")
    55→			t.Logf("deletion commit got checkpoint %s (carry-forward)", cpID2)
    56→		} else {
    57→			t.Log("deletion commit has no checkpoint (deleted files may not carry forward)")
    58→		}
    59→		testutil.AssertNoShadowBranches(t, s.Dir)
    60→	})
    61→}
    62→

    18→// TestRewindPreCommit: agent creates two files in sequence (no user commit),
    19→// then rewinds to the point after the first file was created.
    20→func TestRewindPreCommit(t *testing.T) {
    21→	testutil.ForEachAgent(t, 3*time.Minute, func(t *testing.T, s *testutil.RepoState, ctx context.Context) {
    22→		// Agent creates file A.
    23→		_, err := s.RunPrompt(t, ctx,
    24→			"create a markdown file at docs/red.md with a paragraph about the colour red. Do not ask for confirmation, just make the change.")
    25→		if err != nil {
    26→			t.Fatalf("agent prompt 1 failed: %v", err)
    27→		}
    28→		testutil.AssertFileExists(t, s.Dir, "docs/red.md")
    29→
    30→		pointsAfterA := entire.RewindList(t, s.Dir)
    31→		require.NotEmpty(t, pointsAfterA, "expected at least 1 rewind point after file A")
    32→
    33→		// Agent creates file B.
    34→		_, err = s.RunPrompt(t, ctx,
    35→			"create a markdown file at docs/blue.md with a paragraph about the colour blue. Do not ask for confirmation, just make the change.")

    38→		}

    40→
    41→		pointsAfterB := entire.RewindList(t, s.Dir)
    42→		require.Greater(t, len(pointsAfterB), len(pointsAfterA),
    43→			"expected more rewind points after file B")
    44→
    45→		// Rewind to the first rewind point (after file A was created).
    46→		rewindID := pointsAfterA[0].ID
    47→		err = entire.Rewind(t, s.Dir, rewindID)
    48→		require.NoError(t, err, "rewind to %s should succeed", rewindID)

    59→// invalid after a user commit. Rewinding to an old shadow branch ID should fail.
    60→func TestRewindAfterCommit(t *testing.T) {

    62→		// Agent creates a file.
    63→		_, err := s.RunPrompt(t, ctx,
    64→			"create a markdown file at docs/red.md with a paragraph about the colour red. Do not commit the file. Do not ask for confirmation, just make the change.")
    65→		if err != nil {
    66→			t.Fatalf("agent failed: %v", err)
    67→		}
    68→		testutil.AssertFileExists(t, s.Dir, "docs/red.md")

    71→		pointsBefore := entire.RewindList(t, s.Dir)

    73→
    74→		// Find a non-logs-only point (shadow branch ID).
    75→		var shadowPoint *entire.RewindPoint
    76→		for i := range pointsBefore {
    77→			if !pointsBefore[i].IsLogsOnly {
    78→				shadowPoint = &pointsBefore[i]
    79→				break
    80→			}
    81→		}
    82→		require.NotNil(t, shadowPoint, "expected at least one shadow branch rewind point")
    83→		oldID := shadowPoint.ID

    85→		// User commits the file.

    87→		s.Git(t, "commit", "-m", "Add red.md")
    88→

    92→		pointsAfter := entire.RewindList(t, s.Dir)

    94→		// Verify the old shadow branch ID is no longer listed.
    95→		found := false

    98→				found = true
    99→				break
   100→			}
   101→		}
   102→		assert.False(t, found, "old shadow branch rewind point %s should no longer be listed", oldID)

   105→		err = entire.Rewind(t, s.Dir, oldID)

   111→	})
   112→}

    20→		_, err := s.RunPrompt(t, ctx,

    25→				"Do not ask for confirmation, just make the changes.")
    26→		if err != nil {
    27→			t.Fatalf("agent failed: %v", err)

    29→

    38→
    39→		cpBranchAfterFirst := testutil.GitOutput(t, s.Dir, "rev-parse", "entire/checkpoints/v1")
    40→

    42→		s.Git(t, "commit", "-m", "Add ended file C")
    43→		testutil.WaitForCheckpointAdvanceFrom(t, s.Dir, cpBranchAfterFirst, 15*time.Second)
    44→		cpID2 := testutil.AssertHasCheckpointTrailer(t, s.Dir, "HEAD")

    17→// naturally, user commits still get checkpoint trailers.
    18→func TestEndedSessionUserCommitsAfterExit(t *testing.T) {
    19→	testutil.ForEachAgent(t, 3*time.Minute, func(t *testing.T, s *testutil.RepoState, ctx context.Context) {
    20→		_, err := s.RunPrompt(t, ctx,
    21→			"Create three files: ended_a.go with 'package main; func EndedA() {}', "+
    22→				"ended_b.go with 'package main; func EndedB() {}', "+
    23→				"ended_c.go with 'package main; func EndedC() {}'. "+
    24→				"Create all three files, nothing else. Do not commit. "+
    25→				"Do not ask for confirmation, just make the changes.")
    26→		if err != nil {
    27→			t.Fatalf("agent failed: %v", err)
    28→		}
    29→
    30→		testutil.AssertFileExists(t, s.Dir, "ended_a.go")
    31→		testutil.AssertFileExists(t, s.Dir, "ended_b.go")
    32→		testutil.AssertFileExists(t, s.Dir, "ended_c.go")
    33→
    34→		s.Git(t, "add", "ended_a.go", "ended_b.go")
    35→		s.Git(t, "commit", "-m", "Add ended files A and B")
    36→		testutil.WaitForCheckpoint(t, s, 15*time.Second)
    37→		cpID1 := testutil.AssertHasCheckpointTrailer(t, s.Dir, "HEAD")
    38→
    39→		cpBranchAfterFirst := testutil.GitOutput(t, s.Dir, "rev-parse", "entire/checkpoints/v1")
    40→
    41→		s.Git(t, "add", "ended_c.go")
    42→		s.Git(t, "commit", "-m", "Add ended file C")
    43→		testutil.WaitForCheckpointAdvanceFrom(t, s.Dir, cpBranchAfterFirst, 15*time.Second)
    44→		cpID2 := testutil.AssertHasCheckpointTrailer(t, s.Dir, "HEAD")

    48→		testutil.AssertCheckpointExists(t, s.Dir, cpID2)

    50→	})

53→// TestSessionDepletedManualEditNoCheckpoint tests that once all session files
    54→// are committed, subsequent manual edits do NOT get checkpoint trailers.
    55→func TestSessionDepletedManualEditNoCheckpoint(t *testing.T) {
    56→	testutil.ForEachAgent(t, 2*time.Minute, func(t *testing.T, s *testutil.RepoState, ctx context.Context) {
    57→		_, err := s.RunPrompt(t, ctx,
    58→			"Create a file called depleted.go with content 'package main; func Depleted() {}'. "+
    59→				"Create only this file. Do not commit. "+
    60→				"Do not ask for confirmation, just make the change.")
    61→		if err != nil {
    62→			t.Fatalf("agent failed: %v", err)
    63→		}
    64→
    65→		testutil.AssertFileExists(t, s.Dir, "depleted.go")
    66→
    67→		s.Git(t, "add", ".")
    68→		s.Git(t, "commit", "-m", "Add depleted.go")
    69→		testutil.WaitForCheckpoint(t, s, 15*time.Second)
    70→		cpID := testutil.AssertHasCheckpointTrailer(t, s.Dir, "HEAD")
    71→		testutil.AssertCheckpointExists(t, s.Dir, cpID)
    72→
    73→		cpBranchAfterAgent := testutil.GitOutput(t, s.Dir, "rev-parse", "entire/checkpoints/v1")
    74→
    75→		os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(s.Dir, "depleted.go"),
    76→			[]byte("package main\n\n// Manual user edit\nfunc Depleted() { return }\n"), 0o644)
    77→
    78→		s.Git(t, "add", "depleted.go")
    79→		s.Git(t, "commit", "-m", "Manual edit to depleted.go")
    80→
    81→		time.Sleep(5 * time.Second)
    82→		cpBranchAfterManual := testutil.GitOutput(t, s.Dir, "rev-parse", "entire/checkpoints/v1")
    83→		assert.Equal(t, cpBranchAfterAgent, cpBranchAfterManual,
    84→			"manual edit after session depletion should not advance checkpoint branch")
    85→		testutil.AssertNoCheckpointTrailer(t, s.Dir, "HEAD")
    86→		testutil.AssertNoShadowBranches(t, s.Dir)
    87→	})
    88→}
